summaries.headline: Denver Board, Superintendent Air Tensions at Retreat
summaries.summary: Denver's school board and Superintendent Alex Marrero spent eight hours Monday in a facilitated retreat addressing months of friction, with the sharpest exchange centered on how board members set meeting agendas and get their priorities heard. The session followed a June letter in which Marrero detailed frustrations with board members overstepping into administrative matters and canceling paired meetings with his staff over interpersonal conflicts, tensions that surfaced alongside his since-rejected bid for the Miami superintendent job. Even with the calm tone and one member calling it the board's most collaborative moment yet, the underlying governance disputes—and a superintendent who has twice tested the exit door—suggest Denver's leadership stability remains a work in progress.

summaries.headline: Ed Department Issues Edtech Guidance, Skips Regulation
summaries.summary: The U.S. Department of Education released long-awaited guidance on classroom edtech use, directing states and districts to distinguish "recreational" from "instructional" technology and evaluate tools based on measurable student outcomes rather than access or login frequency. Assistant Secretary Kirsten Baesler's Dear Colleague Letter frames responsible design and product certification as merely "the floor," pushing for deeper evidence about why and for whom a tool works, but the department stopped short of issuing binding federal rules, leaving implementation to states and districts. With no enforcement mechanism attached, the guidance shifts pressure onto district leaders to build their own evaluation standards for a marketplace long criticized for weak evidence behind learning claims.

summaries.headline: California's Literacy Law Faces Implementation Test
summaries.summary: California passed literacy reform legislation last year requiring teachers to be trained in "the science of reading," following a wave of similar laws in dozens of other states that included literacy coaches, professional development and aligned curriculum adoption requirements. The harder work now falls to the California Department of Education, which must review and recommend evidence-based professional development programs that districts can then select from to fulfill the law's mandate. Passing the bill was the easy part — whether California's reform translates into real classroom change depends entirely on how rigorously the state vets and rolls out the programs districts will actually use.

summaries.headline: Colorado's Math Scores Climb, Literacy Splits by Grade
summaries.summary: Colorado's newly released 2026 CMAS results show math proficiency continuing to rise across elementary and middle school, with eighth graders posting the largest year-over-year gains. Literacy told a more divided story: fourth and fifth graders improved in reading and writing, while sixth, seventh, and eighth grade scores declined across the board, with sixth grade proficiency slipping from 44.2% in 2025. Statewide, 44.7% of students met or exceeded expectations in English language arts compared to 37.3% in math, leaving district leaders to reckon with a middle school literacy slide even as elementary gains and math momentum suggest some strategies are gaining traction.

summaries.headline: SEL's Top Job: Friendships, Motivation, Engagement
summaries.summary: Educators lean on social-emotional learning most to tackle student friendship struggles, flagging motivation, and disengagement, according to an EdWeek Research Center survey of 499 teachers, principals, and district leaders conducted in December and January 2026. Bullying and mental health challenges ranked fourth and fifth, while cellphone use and excessive screen time landed near the bottom of all 18 categories despite dominating district-level policy debates. The gap between what's consuming administrative attention and what educators actually deploy SEL to solve suggests schools may be treating tech-related behavior issues as separate from the social-emotional toolkit rather than integrating them.

summaries.headline: CASEL Names New CEO Amid SEL Backlash
summaries.summary: Joshua P. Starr, former PDK International CEO and a onetime district superintendent and classroom teacher, has taken over as chief executive of CASEL, the leading national organization promoting social-emotional learning in schools. Starr steps into the role as SEL faces intensifying political scrutiny and shifting district priorities, arguing that academics alone can't prepare students to navigate an increasingly complex world. His appointment signals how the organization plans to position SEL's next chapter at a moment when the field's messaging, credibility, and staying power in classrooms are all being tested.

summaries.headline: NYC Redesigns Student Survey, Adds Vaping Questions
summaries.summary: New York City overhauled its annual school survey, cutting the number of student questions to 61 from 79 and sharpening the language to get more direct feedback from middle and high schoolers on issues like vaping frequency, bathroom access aligned with gender identity, and whether coursework connects to real-world learning. More than 357,000 students in grades 6-12 responded, a 3-point jump in participation from last year, after officials gathered input from over 300 school leaders and more than 20 students to redesign the questionnaire. Because the changes make this year's results incomparable to prior surveys, district officials are cautioning that lower favorability scores reflect more precise questions rather than declining conditions — leaving school leaders with a fresh baseline to track student experience going forward.

summaries.headline: Pennsylvania Delays Test Scores, Philly Scrambles
summaries.summary: Philadelphia teachers and principals typically receive PSSA and Keystone results by June, but with students returning Aug. 24, educators still have nothing from the 2025-26 school year. The Pennsylvania Department of Education says school-level data went out in June but a "review of preliminary data is still underway," leaving the district unable to use the results for year-over-year achievement comparisons or school selection criteria, and forcing schools to rely on STAR benchmark exams and a fall "alternative assessment" instead. With school selection opening Sept. 8 and no clarity from the state on timing, families and staff are left rostering classes, targeting interventions, and making admissions decisions without the data they've always used to do it.

summaries.headline: Colorado Education Co-op Dissolves After State Scrutiny
summaries.summary: Education reEnvisioned BOCES, the Colorado co-op that authorized "Colorado's first public Christian school" and dozens of publicly funded homeschool enrichment programs, will dissolve over the coming school year after District 49's school board voted unanimously to end the 13-year-old organization. State education officials this month found the co-op had an improperly constituted board, invalid contracts, and misspent state money, following legislative pushback over programs that subsidized ski passes, sports camps, and private school tuition. District 49 will absorb governance and financial oversight during the wind-down, taking over as authorizer for six online schools while parents and program providers warn that students in limbo could become "collateral damage" of the collapse.

summaries.headline: Chicago Moves to Fully Elected School Board
summaries.summary: Chicago voters will elect the city's entire Board of Education this November, ending 30 years of mayoral control over the district. Every registered voter can cast ballots for a representative from their local electoral district and for a board president, a structural overhaul from the mayor-appointed system Richard M. Daley established in 1995 to oversee CPS reform. The shift hands district governance directly to the electorate for the first time in a generation, reshaping who sets priorities and holds CPS leadership accountable going forward.

summaries.headline: ACLU Threatens Lawsuit Over WV School Funding
summaries.summary: The ACLU of West Virginia has announced its intent to sue the state over how it funds public schools, signaling a legal challenge to the current school finance system. Details on the specific funding formula or disparities driving the planned litigation were not disclosed in the announcement, leaving open questions about which districts or student populations the organization argues are most affected. A formal filing would place West Virginia among a growing list of states facing court scrutiny over whether their funding models meet constitutional adequacy and equity standards.

summaries.headline: ACLU Signals New School Funding Lawsuit in WV
summaries.summary: The ACLU of West Virginia notified state officials Monday that it intends to sue on behalf of Lincoln County students, arguing chronic underfunding violates the state constitution's "thorough and efficient" education guarantee and its equal protection provisions. The notice, required 30 days before action against a government agency, names top state officials including the House Speaker, Senate President, and the state education department, and echoes Lincoln County's role in the 1970s and '80s Pauley v. Kelley and Pauley v. Bailey cases that once forced the state's school system to be ruled unconstitutionally inadequate. With that precedent already on the books defining what an adequate education requires in more detail than almost any other state court ruling, district leaders statewide may soon face fresh legal scrutiny over whether funding levels still meet that bar.

summaries.headline: Middle School Literacy Gains Require Structure, Not Programs
summaries.summary: District leaders discovered that middle school students were arriving with unaddressed gaps in decoding, spelling, and fluency, exposing a mismatch between secondary English teachers trained as content experts and students still needing explicit foundational literacy instruction. The fix wasn't a new curriculum purchase but a structural shift: moving literacy from a supplemental "initiative" into scheduled, non-negotiable time through intervention blocks, repurposed advisory periods, or schoolwide "all hands on deck" models, backed by a blended approach including Lexia PowerUp Literacy. The lesson for other districts chasing adolescent literacy gains is that sustained outcomes hinge less on which tool is adopted and more on whether time, staffing, and expectations are restructured to make the work systemic rather than optional.

summaries.headline: Dual Enrollment Grows, But Quality Lags Behind
summaries.summary: Nearly 40% of Colorado's community college enrollment now consists of high schoolers earning college credit, part of a national surge in dual and concurrent enrollment programs. About 78,000 Colorado students took a college-level course in 2025, with roughly 40,000 dual-enrolled at a community college — up more than 3,000 from the previous fall — yet a new Community College Research Center report warns that rapid growth hasn't been matched by stronger program design or clearer pathways to a degree or career. The findings echo concerns Colorado officials have already raised about funding gaps and inconsistent credit value, suggesting that scaling access without addressing structural quality issues could leave many students with credits that don't add up to real progress.

summaries.headline: AI Literacy Emerges as Equity Imperative
summaries.summary: Education researchers argue that as generative AI tools spread through classrooms, schools risk widening equity gaps unless students and teachers develop critical AI literacy alongside technical access. The piece frames AI fluency not just as knowing how to use chatbots or generative tools, but as understanding bias, data provenance, and the ethical stakes embedded in algorithmic systems that increasingly shape learning. Districts that treat AI literacy as a bolt-on tech skill rather than a core component of inclusive, ethical instruction may find their students unprepared to navigate a workforce and civic life already reshaped by these tools.

summaries.headline: California Bill Targets Student Data Sale Loopholes
summaries.summary: California Assemblymember Dawn Addis has introduced AB 1159, legislation designed to close loopholes in state law that currently allow companies to collect and sell young people's personal data. The bill would extend existing K-12 student data privacy protections to college students while preserving access to legitimate scholarship, recruitment, and admissions information. For district leaders navigating vendor contracts and edtech partnerships, the bill signals growing legislative scrutiny of how student data flows to third parties long after students leave the K-12 system.

summaries.headline: BYU Research Sparks Utah Student Privacy Law
summaries.summary: Utah lawmakers passed new student data privacy legislation this session after a Brigham Young University study raised concerns about how districts collect, store, and share student information. Researchers found gaps in oversight and inconsistent safeguards across school systems, prompting policymakers to act on findings that originated in academic research rather than a high-profile breach or vendor complaint. The episode offers a rare example of research translating directly into statute, giving other states a model for how academic findings on data practices can drive concrete policy change.

summaries.headline: Connecticut Doubles Down on Attendance Gains
summaries.summary: Connecticut is investing $7 million to expand its student attendance program even as chronic absenteeism rates show signs of improvement statewide. State leaders are betting that sustained funding, rather than pulling back after early progress, will lock in the gains made since pandemic-era absenteeism spikes. The move signals a broader shift among state policymakers treating attendance recovery as a multi-year commitment rather than a short-term fix.

summaries.headline: Delaware's Funding Overhaul Shifts Power to Local Boards
summaries.summary: Delaware school leaders and advocates used a First State Educate webinar to unpack Senate Bill 302, which moves the state from a position-based funding system toward a hybrid model tied more directly to student needs, with major changes taking effect in fiscal 2028. Panelists said the discretionary share of district funding could jump from about 8% to more than 30%, consolidating roughly 32 funding categories into three tiers covering base staffing, opportunity funding for multilingual and low-income students, and flexible operational dollars. Education Secretary Cindy Marten and board member Brittany Mumford both stressed that this added flexibility comes with sharper accountability, since districts will now have to justify local spending choices that were previously dictated by the state formula.

Ahn Min-seok, Gyeonggi Province Superintendent of Education. Photo courtesy of the Gyeonggi Provincial Office of Education

SUWON — Gyeonggi Province Education Superintendent Ahn Min-suk on the 21st voiced concern over a plan to overhaul the local education grant, announced by the Ministry of Planning and Budget, calling it "a measure that shakes the foundation of the education budget without sufficient discussion."

Ahn criticized the plan as "a step back that reduces the total volume of national education investment," and said it "fails to adequately present the fiscal changes before and after the overhaul, the annual reduction in grants, or the medium- to long-term impact on the country's overall education spending."

The superintendent pointed in particular to the fact that excess revenue from national taxes would not flow through to investment in elementary, middle and high school education. Ahn said the plan "darkens the future of primary and secondary education and does no good for the development of South Korea, whose only competitive edge is cultivating talent."

Ahn agreed on the need to expand the state's responsibility for early childhood education and for higher and lifelong education. But the superintendent said that "reducing funding for compulsory primary and secondary education and moving it to other areas is a zero-sum redistribution — robbing Peter to pay Paul."

Ahn also stressed Gyeonggi Province's particular education circumstances. The province has a large number of students and strong demand for new schools driven by new-town development. Continued investment is also needed to relieve overcrowded classrooms, improve aging education facilities and build future-education infrastructure based on digital technology and AI, the superintendent said.

Ahn said that "cutting the education budget based on the school-age population alone ignores the urgent demands of schools on the ground and the qualitative shift in education."

The superintendent urged the National Assembly to gather the views of the education community and the public and pursue amended legislation. Ahn also emphasized that a stable investment structure for primary and secondary education must be maintained.

The Gyeonggi Provincial Office of Education said it would work to secure funding for primary and secondary education and, together with the Gyeonggi education community, push a "Gyeonggi Education Budget Transformation" for reasonable budget management.

After more than a year of meetings and hundreds of hours of work per person, we’re disappointed to report that the School Funding Interim Commission has fallen short of its legislatively-mandated tasks (House Bill 153, 2025). As members appointed to the Commission, we feel compelled to give the public our frank assessment of where the commission succeeded and where it fell flat.

We were able to identify a number of the student demographics that need better funding mechanisms. We’ve highlighted that the tallying of student populations within districts needs a better system to allocate money to cover the actual costs of providing those students with an education. Special education funding requires more clarity in definitions, and more examination is needed of the growth of base funding and reliance on the state’s General Fund. The Commission also voted to propose several education funding changes that may make improvements on the margins.

However, after spending over $327,000 during this process, the Commission avoided discussion about planning for student academic success, didn’t account for decreasing enrollment trends, and absolutely did not achieve its fundamental goal of creating a simpler, more streamlined, and more effective school funding formula.

Although our property tax system has garnered the moniker as being the most (unnecessarily) complicated in the nation, our school funding formula isn’t far behind. That’s not only a disservice to school administrators and classroom teachers who have to make their budgets and operate within those budgets, it’s also not fair to the taxpayers whose bills depend more on school costs than any other individual type of government service.

We had a lot of input during this process from education-related professional organizations, teachers, and a handful of school board members. Unfortunately, public involvement didn’t include many parents or average citizens worried about their tax burdens and the educational needs of our students.

We hope that efforts by the Legislature and any future School Funding Commission are specifically targeted toward addressing the shortcomings of this Commission and actually achieving the goal of having a school funding formula that is adequate, fair, transparent, understandable, and efficient. Anything less is a disservice to current students and future generations of Montanans.

_Sen. Becky Beard (R-Elliston), Sen. Sue Vinton (R-Billings), and Rep. Lee Deming (R-Laurel) are members of the School Funding Interim Commission._

The Frederick County government and Frederick County Public Schools will co-host three town hall meetings to provide residents with information about an upcoming local sales tax referendum that will appear on the ballot during the November general election, including the early voting period, according to a county media release.

Virginia law allows local jurisdictions to seek voter authorization for an additional local retail sales tax of up to 1% to provide funding that can only be used for the construction or major renovation of public schools. The additional local sales tax is the first and only local school funding tool authorized by the Virginia General Assembly. Previously authorized in select localities, the funding tool was expanded statewide as part of the 2027-2028 Commonwealth of Virginia budget bill.

Frederick County residents will vote on the referendum on Nov. 3 and during the early voting period. The town hall meetings will provide an opportunity for residents to learn more about the proposed funding tool, ask questions, and review the school division’s long-term Capital Improvements Plan (CIP).

The question that will appear on the ballot is:

SHALL FREDERICK COUNTY, VIRGINIA, BE ALLOWED TO ENACT A LOCAL RETAIL SALES TAX OF UP TO ONE PERCENT (1%) TO PROVIDE FUNDS THAT CAN ONLY BE USED FOR CONSTRUCTION OR MAJOR RENOVATION OF PUBLIC SCHOOLS IN FREDERICK COUNTY FOR A PERIOD OF NOT MORE THAN TWENTY YEARS?

If approved by voters, the Board of Supervisors may then enact the new school funding tax. The tax would go into effect 120 days after enactment.

If enacted, the additional sales tax of up to 1% would apply to taxable retail purchases, including items such as clothing, footwear, electronics, and restaurant meals. Essential items such as groceries and personal hygiene products would be excluded from the additional sales tax. Sales tax revenue would be generated not only from Frederick County residents, but also from visitors who shop, dine and otherwise make taxable purchases in the County.

Revenue generated from the proposed tax would be legally restricted to qualifying school construction, major structural renovations, or debt service associated with those projects. Funds cannot be used to pay off existing school construction debt, and the tax would expire after 20 years.

**Town hall dates and locations**

Frederick County residents are invited to attend any of the following sessions:

Thursday, Aug. 27, from 6 to 7 p.m. at Millbrook High School

Tuesday, Sept. 1, from 6 to 7 p.m. at Sherando High School (The meeting will also be livestreamed at [https://www.youtube.com/live/gXe7kLBiY5U](https://www.youtube.com/live/gXe7kLBiY5U))

Tuesday, Sept. 8, from 6 to 7 p.m. at James Wood High School

**School tours**

In addition to the town hall meetings, Frederick County Public Schools will host tours of Apple Pie Ridge Elementary School and Bass-Hoover Elementary School. These schools are among the facilities that could benefit from sales tax revenues if the referendum is approved and the tax is subsequently enacted.

The tours will provide residents with an opportunity to see the schools and learn more about their facility needs.

Wednesday, Sept.  2, at 6 p.m. at Apple Pie Ridge Elementary School

Wednesday, Sept. 9, at 6 p.m. at Bass-Hoover Elementary School

CHARLESTON — The president of the West Virginia Board of Education says an ACLU notice of intent to sue over school funding issues didn’t shock him.

“I am not really surprised by their filing of the notice,” Paul Hardesty told The West Virginia Record in a statement. “This is my fourth term as president of the West Virginia Board of Education. I have repeatedly asked for help with the current outdated school aid funding formula. To date, I have received none.”

On Aug. 17, the American Civil Liberties Union of West Virginia sent the intent to file suit to state officials on behalf of a class of Lincoln County students alleging persistent underfunding of public schools violates the “thorough and efficient” education guarantee and the equal protection provisions of the state constitution.

The notice was sent to state Attorney General J.B. McCuskey, and it listed a host of state officials, including House Speaker Roger Hanshaw, State Senate President Randy Smith, Auditor Mark Hunt, Tax Commissioner Matthew Irby, Treasurer Larry Pack, the state Department of Education, the state Board of Education, the state School Building Authority and others.

Nearly 50 years ago, Lincoln County students brought the landmark case Pauley v. Kelly in which the West Virginia Supreme Court of Appeals established that a thorough and efficient education is a fundamental constitutional right. And in the 1982 Recht decision, a court documented in exhaustive detail how Lincoln County’s schools fell short of that standard and directed the state to fix it.

Now, more than 40 years later, the ACLU says Lincoln County students receive a worse education, across many metrics, than their parents and grandparents did.

“By some measures the schools are worse off than the system a court already found unconstitutional,” the ACLU says in a press release about its intent to sue.

Hardesty cited that 1982 Recht decision.

“It was litigation that came from Lincoln County 44 years ago that forced the courts to weigh in on the school aid formula,” he said. “Now, that outdated, antiquated funding formula will be revisited once again as a result of this pending litigation from Lincoln County.”

ACLU-WV Legal Director Aubrey Sparks said children are guaranteed the right to a thorough and efficient education in the state constitution.

“West Virginia made this promise concrete in 1982, when a court defined, in greater detail than any court in the country before or since, what a thorough and efficient education requires, and what falls short,” Sparks said. “Today, despite the passage of nearly 50 years since this right was first made concrete in the historic Recht decision, Lincoln County students are receiving a lower quality education than what their parents and their grandparents, received before them.

“The West Virginia Constitution does not and should not allow this profoundly important constitutional right to wither and die on the vine as the result of ongoing financial neglect by the defendants.”

The ACLU’s seven-page notice describes a school funding system that it says fails students statewide, with particularly dire effects in Lincoln County where current funding provides basic aid that is wholly insufficient to deliver an adequate education. It says special education receives only minimal state funding — far less than amounts previously deemed unconstitutional.

According to the ACLU, counties are left to bridge the gap, and their ability to do so depends on local property values, producing steep inequities. The gap in per-pupil spending between wealthy and poor counties is now more than three times larger than when that same disparity was declared unconstitutional, the ACLU says.

It also says the staffing formula often funds fewer positions per 1,000 students than the level found insufficient in 1982.

In Lincoln County, the ACLU says those failures translate into shortages of certified and experienced teachers, underfunded special education programs, aging facilities and unnecessary school closures.

In 2021, the Duval PK-8 school was condemned for structural issues. Since then, students in grades 2-8 have been taught in a former career-center building with no exterior windows or natural light in rooms that were once automotive bays and welding shops.

During the 2024-25 school year, no Lincoln County school met the state’s literacy proficiency standards.

“While legal responsibility for the underfunding remains to be determined by a court, the moral responsibility is clear and does not fall equally on every official named, some of whom have themselves publicly urged the state to meet its obligations,” the ACLU statement reads. “The lawsuit will seek declaratory, injunctive, and mandamus relief asking a court to declare the state’s school funding system unconstitutional and to order the state to meet its duty to provide a thorough and efficient education.”

The future of rural education and the impact of school closures were topics discussed during a public education town hall on Thursday in Dingess. Those in attendance expressed concerns about the high number of school closures in southern West Virginia.

Approximately 50 people attended the meeting at the East Fork Volunteer Fire Department, where political leaders, candidates, community members and educators expressed concerns about public education.

“I am a firm believer in keeping our little community schools open. I came here to get some information,” said State Sen. Mark Maynard (R), adding the meeting was productive and he came away with some ideas.

Maynard said he would like to see a moratorium on closing small, public schools.

Wyatt Lilly, Democratic candidate for State Senate District 6, said rural communities should have the same resources as schools in more populated areas.

“People say, ‘Why don’t you just move?’ Well, why should they? Why should they have to? People who live here really like it. People who live in McDowell County really like McDowell County,” Lilly explained.

Lilly added that people who pay taxes in rural areas should receive the same services as people in Beckley or Morgantown.

Seth DiStefano, senior policy outreach director for the West Virginia Center on Budget and Policy, told attendees that it is up to them to keep small, rural schools open.

“Folks understand that school closures are not inevitable,” said DiStefano. “We want communities to know that if the state legislature acts, and they should act, that these closures can be avoided.”

He added that community schools are the “heartbeat” of rural communities in southern West Virginia.

Those in attendance want to see changes to the school funding formula, especially the elimination of the Hope Scholarship that diverts public education funds to private schooling.

“By allowing the money to follow the student, public education is suffering, including small, rural schools,” DiStefano said.

At a press conference held on the 4th of this month in front of Sarangchae at Cheong Wa Dae in Seoul to launch emergency action against the 2026 local education finance grant overhaul, officials from education and civic groups demand an immediate halt to the education grant overhaul. Yonhap News

Teachers, parents and education workers have called on the Presidential Office to keep the formula that links local education funding to 20.79% of national internal taxes, as the government prepares to unveil a plan to overhaul the system. A day after superintendents across the country urged the government to keep the formula, education groups joined in resisting any change to the current funding calculation.

An emergency coalition responding to the reform of the local education grant said it met with a presidential secretary for public engagement on the 20th and conveyed the education sector's concerns and demands about the overhaul the government is pursuing. Teachers, parents, education workers, civic groups and provincial education office officials attended the meeting.

"There has never once been a proper process to listen to the views of superintendents, teachers, parents, education workers and education civic groups, who are the direct parties to education finance reform," the coalition said. "If this is a major policy that changes the basic structure of education finance, the government should have discussed it with the parties involved before drafting the plan and gone through a sufficient process of public debate."

The coalition stressed that the current formula, which allocates 20.79% of national internal taxes as education grants, has been the institutional foundation guaranteeing the stability and predictability of education finance. Even if the government explains that it will not cut the absolute size of next year's education budget, changing the calculation formula that determines the size of future budgets is a separate matter, the group said.

The Ministry of Planning and Budget is reportedly considering scrapping the current method of linking the grant to internal taxes and instead calculating it based on nominal growth and changes in the school-age population, in light of the shrinking number of school-age children. In response, the coalition argued that "if the government's position is that the budget will not shrink, there is no reason to abolish the 20.79% formula," and said a stable financial structure should not be changed based on short-term tax revenue conditions alone.

The coalition also rebutted the use of a declining school-age population as a main basis for the overhaul. While the number of students is falling, it said, the educational demands schools must handle are actually growing, including support for multicultural and immigrant-background students and students eligible for special education, student mental health and counseling, responses to school violence, care and education welfare, AI and digital education, and easing overcrowded classes. In rural and fishing communities, it warned, cutting education funding based on student numbers could shrink schools and lead to worsening conditions for local residents and an acceleration of regional decline.

On a future-response fund the government is considering, the coalition said it "must not take the form of creating a separate fund while damaging the existing structure of the local education grant." It also urged that funding for higher education be secured through a separate, stable source rather than by cutting and transferring the budget for kindergarten, elementary and secondary education.
